## Overview

Backpressure is a flow-control mechanism in streaming pipelines that prevents fast producers from overwhelming slow consumers. Rather than allowing an unbounded buffer to grow until the process exhausts memory, backpressure enables the consumer to signal the producer to reduce its emission rate.

## Common Implementation Patterns

### Bounded Queues with Blocking

The producer adds items to a queue with a fixed maximum size. Once the queue reaches capacity, the producer blocks (suspends) until the consumer drains enough items to free space. This is a straightforward synchronous approach.

### Credit-Based Flow Control

The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send N additional items by issuing "credits." The producer tracks available credits and only sends when it has credits to spend. When credits are exhausted, the producer waits for the consumer to grant more. This pattern decouples the producer and consumer and works well in distributed systems.

### Reactive-Pull Models

Instead of the producer pushing items to the consumer, the consumer requests (pulls) items on its own schedule. The producer responds to pull requests only when capacity is available. This inverts the control flow and naturally implements backpressure: the consumer never receives more than it asks for.

## Significance

Backpressure is essential in streaming and reactive systems to:
- Prevent memory exhaustion when producers and consumers operate at different speeds
- Maintain predictable system behavior under load
- Enable graceful degradation rather than crashes
- Support fair resource sharing in concurrent environments
